comment: Validation oracles: the published specifications whose own examples are the Prism's test content. tools/oracle/gen.py fetches each source at its pinned SHA-256, takes its examples out mechanically (an example is kept only if every address in it is at a domain reserved for documentation, RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, so no real person's address enters the repository), and reads each one with a reference reader written to the source's own grammar. test/oracle/read.test.mjs then holds the Prism's reading (site/card.mjs readItem) to that reading, field by field: a message's title, sender, time and plain words; an event's title, place and start; a card's name; a header's encoded words as the specification says they display; a base64 test vector as it decodes; a CSV example as RFC 4180 reads it; a one-time code message as the WICG report says; an element's accessible name as W3C AccName computes it, graded in the browser on the Web Platform Tests' own cases (test/oracle/name.test.mjs); the items a page shows, read as W3C's own feed example renders them, each article heard by its name; an urgency or scarcity line, as the researchers who found it labelled it, as coercive. gaps: kinds of content the Prism reads that no published specification gives examples of, each with why; no test content is written for them. label: the kind of thing a source's specification says its whole messages and events are (a kind the kind reader names); unsourced: kinds no specification publishes a whole example of, each with why. Nothing here is invented: a new kind of content is added by naming the specification it follows.

gaps.why: How soon a person usually answers is measured over several replies from one sender. No pinned specification gives more than one reply from the same sender (RFC 5322 Appendix A.2 has one each), and a public mailing-list archive would bring real people's timing into the repository, which the no-PII rule keeps out even with names replaced. The Prism does not model it until a specification publishes such an exchange to test it on.

No published specification gives example card numbers: ISO/IEC 7812-1, which defines the issuer prefix and the Luhn check digit, is not freely published, and the networks' test numbers are on their own changing pages. The card detector (site/google/ingest.mjs) has no oracle test until one is pinned.
WhatsApp publishes no definition of its Export chat text format, only help pages on how to export. site/source/exports.mjs reads it, untested by any oracle.

Discord's help pages name the files of a data package (messages/index.json, messages/c<id>/messages.json or .csv) but publish no definition of their fields. Untested by any oracle; its CSV files follow RFC 4180, which is.
LinkedIn's help pages name messages.csv and Connections.csv but publish no definition of their columns. Untested by any oracle; the files follow RFC 4180, which is.
